This page tells you which frequency sweep to give a Palace S-parameter run
for what you want to compute, and what each one cost and gave on one
resonator.

Two words recur. A **full solve** solves the field at one frequency, once
per port. An **adaptive sweep**, `adaptive_tolerance=` in `set_driven`, makes
a few full solves per port, builds a small model from them and evaluates the
model at every frequency you list
([S-parameters with Palace](s-parameters-palace.qmd#the-script)). The
numbers below are from a hanger resonator at 7.36 GHz beside a feedline,
whose resonance shows as a narrow notch in |S21|
([the worked example](#the-hanger-resonator)): $f_0$ is its resonance
frequency, Q its quality factor and $f_0/Q$ its linewidth.

Each row gives the list for `set_driven`; all but the last also set
`adaptive_tolerance=1e-3`.

| You want | Set | On the hanger |
|----------|----------------------|--------------------|
| A broadband response | `[Linear(4e9, 9e9, points=2500)]` | 9 and 4 full solves (ports 1 and 2), 3,940 s. The points are 2.0 MHz apart: none falls in the resonance's notch, and the nearest, 0.68 MHz above $f_0$, shows \|S21\| at −0.94 dB. |
| The $f_0$ and Q of a narrow resonance | `[Linear(4e9, 9e9, points=501), Linear(f0 - w, f0 + w, points=2001)]` with `w = 20 * f0 / Q` | 9 and 4 full solves, 3,948 s. A fit of the notch gives $f_0$ and Q; S21 agrees with the full solves of the last row to 2.4 × 10⁻⁶. |
| The same, when you know $f_0$ | add `Points([f0], full_solve=True)` to that list | 5 and 5 full solves, $f_0$ among them, 3,588 s: the model took 921 s to build instead of 1,190 s. S21 agrees with the row above to 1.4 × 10⁻⁵. |
| A few exact frequencies, without an adaptive sweep | `[Points([...])]`, without `adaptive_tolerance`; near a high-Q resonance also `set_numerical(tolerance=1e-9)` | Every frequency in full, 117 to 119 s each per port: 9 frequencies around $f_0$ took 2,137 s and fit the same notch as the second row. |

For a resonator, start from the second row: one run gives the broadband
response and the resonance, and it needs only a rough $f_0$ and Q to place
the window. The window above spans ±20 linewidths with 50 points per
linewidth. How to give and combine ranges, and how a `full_solve` frequency
shares a frequency with another range, is in
[Dense sampling where it matters](s-parameters-palace.qmd#dense-sampling).

## What a sweep costs {#what-a-sweep-costs}

An adaptive sweep costs two things. The first is its model: the full
solves, which on the hanger took 1,190 s for 9 and 4 of them. The model
covers the lowest to the highest frequency you list, whatever the ranges
between them are, so a dense window does not change how it is built: the
band-and-window sweep and the uniform 2,500 points of the first row chose
the same 9 and 4 full solves.

The second is a fixed time at every listed frequency and port, where Palace
evaluates the model and computes what it writes out for that frequency:
0.548 and 0.555 s on the hanger, and about 0.17 s on the smaller chip of
[S-parameters with Palace](s-parameters-palace.qmd). On the hanger, Palace's
postprocessing took 2,254 s of the 3,948 s band-and-window run. So the
frequencies you list are what the sweep costs. A window keeps them few where
a uniform grid cannot: 10 kHz apart across 4 to 9 GHz would be 500,001
frequencies.

## What to avoid {#what-to-avoid}

### A tighter adaptive tolerance {#a-tighter-adaptive-tolerance}

Keep `adaptive_tolerance=1e-3`. On the hanger, `1e-5` bought no accuracy.
Both ports reached Palace's default cap of 20 full solves before the model
agreed to the tolerance, after 7,428 s, and `driven_result()` refuses such a
run ([the adaptive sweep's limit](s-parameters-palace.qmd#settings-you-may-change)).
With `adaptive_max_samples=40` it converged with 32 and 15 full solves in
8,352 s, 2.1 times the 3,948 s at `1e-3`, and its S21 differed from the
`1e-3` run by at most 3.2 × 10⁻⁶. Both agree with the full solves at
`tolerance=1e-9` to 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ and 2.4 × 10⁻⁶, and the notch fits gave the
same $f_0$, $Q_l$ and $|Q_c|$.

### A very fine uniform grid {#a-very-fine-uniform-grid}

A fine grid across a whole band pays the fixed time at every point. 25,000
points from 4 to 9 GHz, 200 kHz apart, would take the same 1,190 s to build
the model, then 25,000 × (0.544 + 0.556) s = 27,500 s at the frequencies:
28,690 s, about 8 hours, against 3,948 s for the band and the window. This
is projected from the measured costs of the 2,500-point run; the
25,000-point run was not made.

### Full solves at the default tolerance {#full-solves-at-the-default-tolerance}

Near a high-Q resonance, full solves need `set_numerical(tolerance=1e-9)`,
a tighter linear-solver tolerance than the default 10⁻⁶. At the default the
9 frequencies around $f_0$ took 87 to 88 s each per port, but their S21 was
off by up to 4.5 × 10⁻³, most at $f_0$. The notch fitted to them gave
$Q_l$ = 11,056.4, 0.8 % low, and $Q_i$ = 7.219 × 10⁵, 30 % below the
adaptive sweep's 1.036 × 10⁶. At `1e-9` they took 117 to 119 s each and
agree with the adaptive sweep to 2.4 × 10⁻⁶. The adaptive sweep needs no
tighter tolerance: at the default, its S21 is the one that agrees.

### Surface EPR off, to save time {#surface-epr-off}

Leaving `set_surface_epr` out saves little: about 4 %, 0.528 and 0.532 s per
frequency and port instead of 0.548 and 0.555 s, and 3,842 s instead of
3,948 s for the whole run. S21 stayed the same to 1.6 × 10⁻⁹, because the
thin films are computed from the field after the solve.

## The hanger resonator {#the-hanger-resonator}

The worked example is a quarter-wave resonator beside a feedline, as on a
readout line. Near the resonance the resonator takes power from the line,
so |S21| dips in a narrow notch; its width and depth give the Q values. The
layout is built from OrcaPen SC PDK cells:

| Part | Value |
|---|---|
| Feedline | the PDK's `cpw_6_10_6`, a 10 µm signal line in 6 µm gaps, 800 µm between two PDK `launcher`s |
| Ports | an 85 × 150 µm port sheet behind each launcher's 150 µm pad; two 50 Ω `LumpedPort`s to `ground`, the left one port 1 |
| Resonator | the PDK `resonator()` at its defaults: 4000 µm of `cpw_6_10_6`, shorted at one end and open at the other, with a 200 µm coupling straight beside the feedline and 5 µm of ground between their gaps |
| Nets | `signal`, the feedline and the launchers; `ground`, the ground plane and the resonator, which is shorted to it |
| Die | 1870 × 2058 µm of silicon, 500 µm thick, with 0.1 µm of aluminium (the PDK's single-die stack) |
| Surface EPR | the PDK's `LiteratureCentral` MA, MS and SA presets |
| Model | metal as solids ([Route B](../concepts/routes.qmd)), second-order elements, 521,337 tetrahedra and 3,677,860 unknowns; Palace with 8 MPI processes |

The plan is built as in sections 1 and 2 of
[the S-parameter script](s-parameters-palace.qmd#the-script), for this
layout. The sweep is the band and the window, placed from the resonator
mode of an Eigenmode run of the same plan:

```python
from scgsim.palace import DrivenSim, Linear

# The resonator mode of the Eigenmode run.
f0, q = 7.356647804e9, 13947.6
w = 20 * f0 / q  # 20 linewidths, 10.55 MHz

sim = DrivenSim()
sim.set_plan(plan.prepare())
sim.set_driven(
    [
        # The band, 10 MHz apart.
        Linear(4e9, 9e9, points=501),
        # The window, 10.55 kHz apart.
        Linear(f0 - w, f0 + w, points=2001),
    ],
    adaptive_tolerance=1e-3,
)
```

That Q is 25 % too high ([below](#check-against-eigenmode)), yet the window
still spans ±16 of the resonance's true linewidths: a rough Q is enough.

**The fit.** SCGSim gives you S21; fitting the notch is yours. Here it is
the hanger model of
[Probst et al., Rev. Sci. Instrum. 86, 024706 (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4907935),
fitted to S21 at the 2,003 listed frequencies inside the window:

$$
S_{21}(f) = a\,e^{i\alpha}\,e^{-2\pi i f\tau}
\left[1 - \frac{(Q_l/|Q_c|)\,e^{i\phi}}{1 + 2iQ_l\,(f/f_0 - 1)}\right],
$$

$$
\frac{1}{Q_i} = \frac{1}{Q_l} - \frac{\cos\phi}{|Q_c|}.
$$

$Q_l$, the loaded Q, sets the notch's width $f_0/Q_l$. $Q_c$, the coupling
Q, counts the power the resonator gives to the feedline, and $Q_i$, the
internal Q, the power lost inside the model. The line's delay τ, 14.64 ps,
is taken from the phase of the band away from the resonance and removed
before the fit.

| | Band and window | 9 full solves at `tolerance=1e-9` |
|---|---:|---:|
| $f_0$ | 7.356663911 GHz | 7.356663906 GHz |
| $Q_l$ | 11,140.8 | 11,140.8 |
| $\lvert Q_c\rvert$ | 11,261.8 | 11,261.8 |
| $Q_i$ | 1.036 × 10⁶ | 1.036 × 10⁶ |
| Frequencies | 2,502 | 9 |
| Full solves per port | 9 and 4 | 9 and 9 |
| Time | 3,948 s | 2,137 s |
| Peak memory | 35,738 MB | 34,233 MB |

At the 9 frequencies both hold, their S21 agrees to 2.4 × 10⁻⁶. The full
solves cost less here because they are only 9 frequencies; they give no
broadband response, and you must know $f_0$ to place them.

$Q_i$ comes from a small difference between $1/Q_l$ and the coupling's
share, so small errors in S21 move it the most
([an example](#full-solves-at-the-default-tolerance)). It holds the losses
inside the solve. The thin films' surface loss is not among them, as S21
with Surface EPR off shows ([above](#surface-epr-off)); that loss comes from
the Surface EPR rows
([Surface participation](s-parameters-palace.qmd#surface-participation)).

## Check against Eigenmode {#check-against-eigenmode}

An Eigenmode run of the same plan, with the two ports as 50 Ω loads, finds
the resonator's mode directly
([Resonant modes with Palace](modes-palace.qmd)). On the hanger, 4 modes
from 6.5 GHz took 1,431 s, and the resonator was mode 1:

| Compare | Eigenmode | Notch fit |
|--------------------|----------:|----------:|
| $f_0$ | 7.356647804 GHz | 7.356663911 GHz |
| The coupling: $Q_\text{ext}$ of the two ports together, and $\lvert Q_c\rvert$ | 11,258.2 | 11,261.8 |
| The mode's Q at `tolerance=1e-9`, and $Q_l$ | 11,141.7 | 11,140.8 |

- **$f_0$** agrees to 16.1 kHz, 2.2 ppm, at the default tolerance; at
  `tolerance=1e-9` the mode is at 7.356663931 GHz, 20 Hz from the notch's.
- **Compare Q through the coupling Q.** Palace gives each port's
  $Q_\text{ext}$, the Q the mode would have if that port were its only
  loss; the two ports together give
  $1/Q_\text{ext} = 1/Q_{\text{ext},1} + 1/Q_{\text{ext},2}$. It is accurate
  at the default tolerance: 11,258.2, within 0.03 % of $|Q_c|$.
- **Or through the mode's Q, with a tighter linear tolerance.** The Q Palace
  computes from the mode's complex frequency needs
  `set_numerical(tolerance=1e-9)` for a high-Q mode. The imaginary part of
  that frequency is tiny next to its real part, so the solver's approximate
  linear solves move it far more than they move the frequency: at the
  default it gave 13,947.6 here, 25 % high. At `1e-9` it agrees with $Q_l$ to 0.008 %, and
  $1/Q - 1/Q_{\text{ext},1} - 1/Q_{\text{ext},2}$ gives
  $Q_i$ = 1.036 × 10⁶, the notch's.

Palace completes such a run, but SCGSim does not yet read back an Eigenmode
run whose lumped ports are all resistive
([open issue](https://github.com/NCUPHY-LTLab/scgsim/issues/311)):
`resolve_palace_result` marks it failed. Until it does, read the mode from
`results/palace/eig.csv` and each port's $Q_\text{ext}$ from
`results/palace/port-Q.csv` in the run folder.

The runs and their raw numbers are in the
[run record](https://github.com/NCUPHY-LTLab/scgsim/issues/307#issuecomment-7194872828).
